A VLAN: splitting the switch into several

Until now, all the stations on a switch were in the same broadcast domain. We want to build two separate networks, for example development and production, with the same switch.

A VLAN is a virtual LAN: ports are associated with a VLAN and those ports behave «as if they were» a completely separate switch, with their own broadcast domain.

A message is copied to the ports of its VLAN, but doesn't reach the other side.
Isolation lets one group neither see nor share the other's traffic; a provider uses it to separate its clients.
To go from one VLAN to another: a router

VLANs isolate networks. If we still want two VLANs to communicate, a network layer device is needed: the router, which allows passage from one network to the other.

When a station wants to communicate with another on the other VLAN, it sends the message to the router. The router analyzes the frame, reads the destination address and sends the message to the other network.
Within a VLAN the switch does the switching (data link layer); between VLANs the router decides (network layer).
Extending a VLAN to another switch

A user on a VLAN needs more ports, and the switch already has them all in use. Another switch has to be used and the requested ports assigned there.

A first alternative: connect a port on one switch to a port on the other, both in the same VLAN.

It works, but many ports are used up, and it gets worse if one cable per VLAN has to be connected for each VLAN you want to extend.
One link per VLAN doesn't scale: ports run out before VLANs do.
Two VLANs = two cables and four ports in use. Each new VLAN adds another pair.
802.1Q trunk: one cable for all VLANs

The convenient alternative is 802.1Q or VLAN tagging, which turned into a standard what each manufacturer used to solve in its own way.

One port on each switch that doesn't belong to any VLAN is taken and they are connected: that is a trunk.

  • On entering the trunk, the switch adds to the frame a tag indicating which VLAN it belongs to.
  • On arrival, the other switch reads the tag, removes it and copies the frame to the ports of that VLAN.
The trunk lets members of the same VLAN be on another physical device.

The switch has its table with the MAC addresses and their location. If the destination is on the other switch, the frame goes out the 802.1Q port.

To pass through the trunk, a 4-byte tag field is added, inserted between the source address and the Type/Len.

The tag only exists between 802.1Q ports: the stations keep sending and receiving the usual Ethernet frame.
The rest of the frame is untouched: the tag is slipped in and later removed.
Original frame: … SA · Type/Len · Data … On the trunk: … SA · Tag (4 bytes) · Type/Len · Data … On leaving the trunk the tag is removed and the original is restored.
Inside the tag: ethertype, PRI and VLAN-ID

• A new ethertype, different from the Type/Len, with the value 0x8100: it indicates that what follows is a tag. When it is removed, the original Type/Len is back.
  • PRI: used by another protocol, 802.1p, to give one frame priority over another and thus improve quality of service.
  • VLAN-ID: the VLAN number. With 12 bits it allows 4096 combinations.
All that tells one VLAN from another on the trunk is the 12 bits of the VLAN-ID.
2 bytes of ethertype + 3 bits of PRI + 1 flag bit + 12 bits of VLAN-ID = 32 bits. 2¹² = 4096 possible VLANs (0 to 4095).
A trunk to the router or a server

Each client on the switch wants to reach the Internet. With one port per VLAN, 100 VLANs would need a router with 100 interfaces and 100 cables.

The other alternative: one 802.1Q port connected to the router. Over that single physical port arrive the frames of all the VLANs, each with its tag, and the router tags the ones it sends back.

It works for any device that needs that separation, for example a virtual machine server where each VLAN has its own set of VMs.
One 802.1Q port is enough to extend VLANs or give them a resource, without using up a port per VLAN.
With a trunk, 100 VLANs come in through a single port on the router.
The shared cable is a bottleneck

On a switch each station has its own 10 Mbps full-duplex cable. But the cable linking two switches is used by everyone: the capacity is no longer for one station, it is for all.

Whenever a shared resource appears, capacity tends to be lower. Traffic becomes unbalanced.

What if we add a second cable between the switches? You can't just do that: it forms a loop, and Spanning Tree blocks one of the two ports.
Adding a parallel cable doesn't add capacity: STP leaves it blocked.
LACP: several ports, one logical port

LACP (Link Aggregation Control Protocol) tells the switch to treat those ports as a single logical port. If to the switch it is a single link, there is no loop.

It lets you take several ports, up to 8, and build a group that looks like a single port.

This avoids the bottleneck of sending everything over one cable and increases capacity. It also works for 802.1Q: with several ports you build one big trunk.
Physically it's several cables; logically, just one. That's why Spanning Tree blocks nothing.
LACP group: up to 8 ports that the switch treats as one. Adds capacity without forming a loop.

• VLAN: ports on a switch grouped as if they were a separate switch. One broadcast domain per VLAN.
  • To connect VLANs you need a router.
  • 802.1Q trunk: a port that carries all the VLANs; it tags on entry and removes the tag on exit.
  • 4-byte tag between SA and Type/Len: ethertype 0x8100, PRI (802.1p) and VLAN-ID (4096 values).
  • LACP: up to 8 ports as one logical port, more capacity and no loop.

With this we close out wired LANs. In the next unit the shared medium is the air: Wireless LAN and 802.11.
The frame traveling over a trunk: the usual one, plus 4 bytes saying which VLAN it belongs to.
